newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition scores victories over Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition scores victories over Milosevic.

text.p: Serbia's opposition activists secured a double breakthrough on Tuesday in their struggle with President Slobodan Milosevic when their control over Belgrade and the country's second city Nis was reinstated.

Electoral officials in the capital overruled a district court to award victory to the opposition Zajedno coalition in the Belgrade assembly. Zajedno confirmed a court in Nis had made a similar ruling to return full control to Zajedno there.
The reinstatement of Zajedno victories came in the heat of a fierce power struggle among moderates and hardliners in the ruling leftist coalition.

"The decision is chiefly the result of infighting between hardliners and moderates within the (allied Socialist Party) SPS and JUL (Yugoslav United Left)," Milan Bozic, political adviser to Zajedno co-leader Vuk Draskovic, said.
Zajedno's victories signalled that moderates were gaining an upper hand but apparently at a steep price.
Nebojsa Covic, the SPS mayor of Belgrade, who had backed Zajedno demands, paid for his disloyalty.

He and hardline Nis party leader Mile Ilic, the first to resort to election fraud which diplomats say set the pattern across the country, were expelled from the SPS on Tuesday afternoon, state radio Belgrade reported.
The chief of Belgrade socialists Branislav Ivkovic was replaced by Serbian parliament speaker Dragan Tomic.
It was unclear whether Tomic, who angered the protesters by calling them "fascists', would retain his parliament post.

The moves came just hours after some half a million people braved freezing temperatures to jam Belgrade for an Orthodox New Year's Eve protest that was the biggest yet mounted against Milosevic in a campaign to force the Socialist government to reinstate November municipal election results in 14 cities.
"It is truly important news indeed," said political analyst Zarko Korac, referring to the electoral officials' decision.

Opposition activists vowed to keep up that pressure and again insisted they wanted the authorities to restore all their victories as endorsed by factfinders from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"We shall not be satisfied before all the results from November 17 are recognised," Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader, told Reuters Television.
"We shall continue to protest until we get what we have really achieved in Serbia by the votes of the people," he said.
Rival Serbian factions began to line up cautiously behind decisions on Tuesday restoring their victories.
"Because of our bad experiences with the Socialists, we do not trust them," said Slobodan Vuksanovic, spokesman for the opposition Democratic Party.
"I remain cautious because there are 48 hours during which appeals against the decision can be made," Vesna Pesic, another Zajedno leader, told a news conference in Paris.
Moderate leaders of the ruling left coalition backed the electoral decision saying the rule of law was being respected.
Dusan Mihajlovic, a leader of the moderate New Democracy party allied with the Socialists, warned the hardliners not to appeal against Zajedno's victory in Belgrade.
"The Socialists can file a complaint to the electoral commission...But I think that using these legal means would not be politically wise and correct..."

Distancing his party from the SPS-JUL coalition, Mihajlovic promised to walk out of a discussion panel organised by the Serbian government to formulate new electoral rules until election results were restored and Zajedno joined the debate.
The biggest blow to the hardliners came from JUL, headed by Milosevic's wife, who urged its backers to accept the Belgrade electoral commission's action.

"It was a decision reached not on the basis of any political deals but simply one founded on the law, the constitution and insight into the electoral process which took place on November 17," JUL spokesman Alexsandar Vulin said.

Those results awarded 60 seats to the Zajedno (Together) coalition, 23 to the ruling Socialist party (SPS) and allied Yugoslav United Left (JUL), 15 to the Serbian Radical Party and two to the Democratic Party of Serbia.
Votes for the 10 remaining seats are still to be contested but could not jeopardise Zajedno's majority.
